body_md: A `Future` must stay put in memory while polled, so `Pin<&mut F>` promises it will not move. `Box::pin` heap-pins; stack futures need `pin!`. Never call `mem::swap` on a pinned future.
hook: Async futures cannot move once polled — Pin enforces that.
output: // needs futures crate: block_on polls fut to completion → n == 42

quiz.explain: Async fns compile to state machines that may borrow their own fields. Pin guarantees the future stays put, so those borrows stay valid.
options: Pin makes any future Send across threads
It stops a self-referential future moving
Pin cancels the future if it is moved
Pin lets the executor poll it on many threads

takeaway: Pin async futures before polling so self-references stay valid across awaits.
trap: Moving a self-referential future after polling invalidates internal pointers.

body_md: Structs holding pinned futures need **pin projection**: map `Pin<&mut Self>` to `Pin<&mut field>` via `pin_project` crate or manual unsafe. Never project by plain mutable access — use the projected pin.
hook: A struct with a pinned field needs projection, not plain access.
output: // compiles with pin_project: Pin<&mut Wrapper<F>> → Pin<&mut F>

quiz.explain: Projection maps a pin of the struct to pins of its fields (e.g. via pin-project) without moving them; moving a field out breaks Pin.
options: Turning Pin<&mut Self> into Pin<&mut field>
Unpinning every field so each can move freely
Cloning a pinned future into a new slot
Moving a field out of a pinned struct

takeaway: Project pins structurally instead of moving fields out of pinned structs.
trap: Using get_mut to reach inside a pinned struct silently breaks the pin promise.

body_md: **Variance** decides if `&'a T` shrinks to `&'b T`. Shared refs are covariant, `Cell<T>` is invariant, `fn(T)` flips inputs contravariantly. Invariance errors often mean interior mutability blocks shrinking.
hook: Why does &'a T coerce but Cell<T> refuse? Variance.
output: // compiles: 'a: 'b lets &'a str shrink to &'b str (covariance)

quiz.explain: &'a T is covariant, so a longer lifetime can shrink to a shorter one. Cell<T> allows mutation, so it is invariant and refuses.
options: Every generic type is covariant in its T
Every generic type is contravariant in T
&T is covariant, Cell<T> is invariant
Variance only applies inside async code

takeaway: Read invariance errors as interior mutability blocking safe lifetime shrinking.
trap: Storing covariant refs inside invariant cells surprises lifetime shortening.

body_md: **Drop check** ensures a value cannot be dropped while borrows it owns still live. Generic `struct S<T>(T)` gets extra rules; `#[may_dangle]` (unsafe) relaxes them. Keep owned data drop-safe by avoiding borrowed fields.
hook: Drop check: your destructor might outlive its borrows.
output: // compiles: Owner<'a> cannot outlive the String it borrows

quiz.explain: If a type's Drop could touch borrowed data, drop check requires that data to strictly outlive it, so the destructor never sees freed memory.
options: It detects memory leaks at compile time
Data a value borrows must outlive its drop
It counts allocations freed by each drop
It checks that dropped values are Send + Sync

takeaway: Design owning types so destructors never outlive the borrows they hold.
trap: Adding a Drop impl to a borrowing type triggers unexpected drop-check errors.

body_md: `MaybeUninit<T>` reserves uninitialized memory you fill before reading. Pattern: `let mut slot = MaybeUninit::uninit(); ptr.write(val); slot.assume_init()`. Never read before init — that is instant UB.
hook: Uninitialized memory without UB? MaybeUninit, used exactly right.
output: // v == 7: write() fully initializes; assume_init() is sound here

quiz.explain: Reading uninitialized memory is undefined behavior. assume_init only asserts the value is ready; it does not zero or check anything.
options: Write the value fully before assume_init
Reading before writing returns zeroes
assume_init zero-fills unwritten bytes
It drops the inner T at end of scope

takeaway: Write every MaybeUninit slot fully before reading it as initialized.
trap: Reading uninitialized slots even to debug-print triggers undefined behavior.

body_md: `MaybeUninit::zeroed()` is only valid when all-zero bits are legal (ints, not refs). Prefer `uninit()` plus explicit writes. `assume_init` on padding or enums with invalid bit patterns is UB.
hook: Zeroed is not always valid — all-zero bits can still be UB.
output: // b == [0u8; 64]: whole array written before assume_init()

quiz.explain: Integers accept all-zero bits, but references, NonNull, and many enums do not, so assume_init on zeroed memory for those is UB.
options: For any type, since zero is always safe
For any type that does not implement Drop
Only when T is Copy and fits in a register
Only when all-zero bits form a valid T

takeaway: Use zeroed only for types where all-zero bits form a legal value.
trap: Zeroing a reference or bool-like enum creates invalid bit patterns silently.

body_md: `#[repr(C)]` fixes field order for FFI, `repr(packed)` removes padding but makes unaligned access UB on read. Check size with `size_of::<T>()`. Prefer explicit padding fields over packed for perf.
hook: Your struct is bigger than its fields — padding did that.
output: // passes: size_of::<Header>() == 8 (1 tag + 3 pad + 4 len)

quiz.explain: Default Rust layout may reorder fields. repr(C) follows C's rules, giving a stable layout for FFI; repr(packed) is what removes padding.
options: It shrinks structs by reordering fields
It fixes field order and layout for FFI
It removes all padding between fields
It lets a struct inherit C struct fields

takeaway: Choose explicit representations for foreign interfaces and measure padding effects.
trap: Reading packed fields by reference creates unaligned references and UB.

body_md: Atomics take `Ordering`: `Relaxed` for counters, `Acquire`/`Release` for handoff, `SeqCst` for total order (slowest). Match load/store pairs: release-store pairs with acquire-load to publish data safely.
hook: Relaxed versus SeqCst can be a 10x gap — pick deliberately.
output: // passes: Release store pairs with the Acquire load

quiz.explain: Writes before a Release store become visible to a thread whose Acquire load reads that value, which safely publishes data.
options: A Release store syncs with an Acquire load
Relaxed gives all threads one global order
SeqCst is fastest, so use it by default
Ordering only matters on weak ARM chips
quiz.q: How do Release and Acquire pair?

takeaway: Pair release stores with acquire loads and reserve SeqCst for global order.
trap: Using Relaxed for flag handoff lets readers see stale data.

body_md: `compare_exchange(expected, desired, ok, fail)` loops until the atomic matches: the lock-free retry pattern. Use `compare_exchange_weak` in loops (allows spurious fail, faster on ARM). Back off under contention.
hook: Compare-exchange loops: no mutex, just retry until it sticks.
output: // fetch_add returns 0, counter becomes 1 (AcqRel for R-M-W)

quiz.explain: Read the current value, compute the new one, and compare_exchange; if another thread changed it first, retry with the fresh value.
options: Lock a spinlock, then update the value
Disable interrupts around the update
Loop compare_exchange until it succeeds
fetch_add with SeqCst, then validate it
quiz.q: What is the lock-free retry pattern?

takeaway: Build lock-free updates with compare-exchange loops plus backoff under contention.
trap: Spinning without backoff on contended atomics burns CPU and slows everyone.

body_md: **Intrusive** lists store next/prev pointers inside nodes, avoiding allocator churn. Great for kernels and async runtimes. Cost: unsafe link management plus pinned nodes that must never move.
hook: Intrusive lists: zero-alloc linking by storing pointers in nodes.
output: // compiles: Node { next: *mut Node, value: u32 } (unsafe links)

quiz.explain: Intrusive nodes carry their own next/prev pointers, so linking needs no separate allocation. The cost is unsafe code and pinned nodes.
options: They use a garbage collector to free nodes
They keep every node on the stack only
They rely on Rc to share node ownership
Links live in nodes, avoiding allocations

takeaway: Use intrusive lists for zero-allocation linking when unsafe costs are justified.
trap: Moving a linked intrusive node invalidates neighbor pointers instantly.

body_md: Implement `GlobalAlloc` to swap allocators: `#[global_allocator] static A: MyAlloc;`. You must provide `alloc` and `dealloc` with correct layout handling. Measure first — default is excellent for most apps.
hook: GlobalAlloc: replace every allocation in your program.
output: // compiles: Mine delegates to System; set as #[global_allocator] to use

quiz.explain: A static with #[global_allocator] implementing GlobalAlloc serves every heap allocation; only one is allowed per binary.
options: Replaces the allocator for the whole program
Sets a custom allocator for one struct type
Disables heap use so only the stack remains
Picks an allocator at compile time per crate

takeaway: Swap global allocators through GlobalAlloc only after measuring real bottlenecks.
trap: A buggy custom allocator corrupts every allocation and defies debugging.

body_md: `jemalloc` shines for multithreaded servers with many small allocations. Enable via `tikv-jemallocator`, set `MALLOC_CONF` for background threads and dirty-page decay. Benchmark before and after — it can also regress.
hook: jemalloc cut our tail latency 30 percent — then we tuned decay.
output: // with tikv-jemallocator: #[global_allocator] static ALLOC: Jemalloc

quiz.explain: jemalloc's per-thread arenas suit many small allocations across threads, but it can regress some workloads, so measure before and after.
options: Always: it beats every system allocator
On embedded targets with very tight RAM
Threaded servers, confirmed by benchmarks
Only in programs that never spawn threads

takeaway: Trial jemalloc for threaded servers and tune decay only with benchmarks.
trap: Enabling jemalloc without measuring can regress latency on small binaries.

body_md: LLVM **autovectorizes** simple loops into SIMD when it sees contiguous access, no aliasing, and known counts. Help it: use iterators, `slice::chunks_exact`, and `#[inline]`. Check output with `cargo asm` or godbolt.
hook: Autovectorization: four floats per instruction, if loops allow.
output: // compiles: sum(&[f32]) via iterators (autovectorizable)

quiz.explain: LLVM vectorizes when data is contiguous, unaliased, and branch-light. Pointer chasing, hash lookups, and branchy code block it.
options: Linked-list walks with pointer chasing
Simple loops over contiguous slices
Loops that look up keys in a HashMap
Loops with many data-dependent branches

takeaway: Write simple contiguous loops so the compiler can emit SIMD instructions.
trap: Hidden aliasing and branches silently block autovectorization.

body_md: `criterion` reports median, slope, and outliers — not just one timing. Compare baselines with `cargo bench` HTML reports. Watch for bimodal plots (throttling) and keep benchmarks on quiet machines.
code:
use criterion::{criterion_group, criterion_main, Criterion};
fn b(c: &mut Criterion) { c.bench_function("sum", |b| b.iter(|| 1 + 1)); }
hook: Your benchmark improved 5 percent? Criterion says that is noise.
output: // with criterion: benches sum(); statistics, not single timings

quiz.explain: Criterion runs many samples, reports confidence intervals, and compares to a saved baseline, so a 5% blip can be called noise.
options: Statistics tell real changes from noise
It runs the code once for a clean timing
It also verifies results are correct
It turns off optimization for fairness
quiz.q: Why use criterion over a timer?

takeaway: Judge speedups with criterion statistics instead of single timing runs.
trap: Benchmarking on a busy laptop produces bimodal noise mistaken for regressions.

body_md: Capture with `cargo flamegraph`, then read top-down: wide boxes are hot, tall stacks show call chains. Look for unexpected `memcpy`, locking, or allocator frames dominating width. Optimize the widest plateau first.
code:
$ cargo install flamegraph
$ cargo flamegraph --bench mybench
# open flamegraph.svg in browser
hook: The widest box in the flamegraph is where your CPU went.
output:
// cargo flamegraph --bench mybench
// → flamegraph.svg: optimize the widest plateau first

quiz.explain: Width is the share of samples, so wide plateaus are where CPU time goes. Height is just call depth; colors are usually arbitrary.
options: The tallest stacks are the hottest code
Colors mark which functions have bugs
The narrowest boxes are the bottlenecks
The widest boxes take the most CPU time
quiz.q: How do you read a flamegraph?

takeaway: Optimize the widest flamegraph plateau before touching narrow stacks.
trap: Optimizing a tall narrow stack ignores the wide frame eating real cycles.

body_md: `perf stat` shows cycles, cache misses, and branch mispredicts per run. High miss rates mean layout or prefetch issues, not just slow code. Pair with `perf record` for per-symbol hotspots on Linux.
code:
$ perf stat -d ./target/release/app
# watch cache-misses and branch-misses
hook: Cycles lie, cache misses confess — perf stat tells which.
output: // perf stat -d: cycles plus cache-misses and branch-misses per run

quiz.explain: perf stat reads CPU counters (cycles, cache misses, branch mispredicts) that explain why code is slow, not just that it is.
options: Line-by-line timing of each source line
CPU counters like cache and branch misses
Heap allocation counts per function
Lock contention per mutex in the program
quiz.q: What does perf stat add beyond timing?

takeaway: Check hardware counters with perf stat before rewriting hot code paths.
trap: Tuning instructions while cache misses dominate wastes optimization effort.

body_md: `lto = true` enables whole-program optimization; `codegen-units = 1` trades slower builds for better inlining. Set them in `[profile.release]`. Keep dev profiles fast and only ship tuned release builds.
code:
[profile.release]
lto = true
codegen-units = 1
strip = true
hook: LTO: 10% faster binary, 3x slower build. Worth it?
output:
# release: LTO + one codegen unit + stripped
# → faster binary, much slower builds (release only)

quiz.explain: LTO optimizes across crate boundaries and one codegen unit gives LLVM the whole crate at once: better inlining, longer compiles.
options: They make debug builds compile faster
They shrink the source before compiling
Slower builds in exchange for faster code
They turn off inlining to cut binary size
quiz.q: What do LTO and single codegen units do?

takeaway: Enable link-time optimization for release binaries while keeping dev builds fast.
trap: Enabling full LTO in dev profiles makes every iteration painfully slow.

body_md: `sccache` shares compiled crates across builds and machines via Redis or S3. Set `RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache` and warm the cache in CI. Watch hit rates — misses on new toolchains are expected.
code:
$ export RUSTC_WRAPPER=sccache
$ sccache --show-stats
hook: Never compile serde twice again — share it with sccache.
output: // sccache --show-stats: hit rates climb; misses on new toolchains are normal

quiz.explain: sccache wraps rustc via RUSTC_WRAPPER and stores compiled outputs locally or in S3/Redis, so CI and teammates reuse them.
options: Formats code across the whole workspace
Caches compiled crates across builds
Lints unsafe blocks in dependencies
Signs release binaries for distribution

takeaway: Share compilation artifacts with sccache to speed up team and CI builds.
trap: Expecting cache hits across compiler upgrades ignores toolchain-keyed invalidation.

body_md: `cargo deny` and `cargo audit` scan licenses, advisories, and banned crates. Run `cargo audit` in CI and pin a policy file. Treat new RUSTSEC advisories like failing tests — fix or document exceptions.
code:
$ cargo install cargo-audit
$ cargo audit
$ cargo deny check
hook: cargo audit: a dependency has a CVE and CI stayed green?
output: // cargo audit + deny: scan advisories/licenses; treat hits as failures

quiz.explain: cargo audit checks Cargo.lock against the RustSec advisory DB; cargo deny adds license, ban, and source policies. Fail CI on hits.
options: Security advisories and license policy
Unused dependencies and slow link times
Formatting and lint rules in Cargo.toml
Whether every public item has doc comments
quiz.q: What do cargo audit and deny check?

takeaway: Scan dependencies for advisories in CI and treat warnings as failures.
trap: Ignoring advisory warnings for months ships known vulnerabilities to users.

body_md: **Reproducible builds** produce bit-identical binaries from the same sources: pin toolchains with `rust-toolchain`, lock deps, strip paths, and set `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`. Verify by rebuilding in two containers and diffing hashes.
code:
[toolchain]
channel = "1.78"
components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"]
hook: Same source, different hash? Your build is not reproducible.
output: # rust-toolchain pins channel 1.78 with rustfmt + clippy

quiz.explain: Bit-identical output needs identical inputs: a pinned rust-toolchain, Cargo.lock, remapped paths, and a fixed SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH.
options: Incremental caching between every rerun
Skipping tests so results stay stable
Pinned toolchain, deps, paths, and time
Cleaning target/ before every build

takeaway: Pin toolchains and dependencies so release binaries rebuild bit-identically.
trap: Embedding absolute paths and timestamps breaks hash equality across machines.

body_md: **PGO** feeds real profiles back into LLVM: build with `-Cprofile-generate`, run a representative workload, rebuild with `-Cprofile-use`. Hot paths get better inlining and layout. Automate the three-step flow in release CI.
code:
$ RUSTFLAGS="-Cprofile-generate=/tmp/pgo" cargo build --release
# run workload, then rebuild with -Cprofile-use
hook: PGO: let production traffic teach LLVM to optimize.
output: // PGO: build with -Cprofile-generate, run workload, rebuild with -Cprofile-use

quiz.explain: PGO builds an instrumented binary, runs a representative workload, then rebuilds with that profile to guide inlining and layout.
options: A build with optimizations off for profiling
Rebuilding with real runtime profile data
Profiling only the test suite for hot code
A replacement for benchmarking releases

takeaway: Apply profile-guided optimization to hot binaries using representative workloads.
trap: Training PGO on toy inputs mis-optimizes the paths production actually hits.

body_md: Track heap with `dhat`, `massif`, or allocator stats before guessing. Watch peak bytes, churn per request, and fragmentation. Fix arenas, pooling, or `jemalloc` tuning based on numbers — not vibes.
code:
$ valgrind --tool=dhat ./target/release/app
# inspect peak heap and hot alloc sites
hook: Memory high but CPU idle? Profile the heap, not the code.
output: // valgrind --tool=dhat: peak heap bytes plus hot allocation sites

quiz.explain: Tools like dhat and massif track peak bytes, churn, and which call sites allocate most, so you fix memory with data, not guesses.
options: Peak usage and hot allocation sites
Which functions use the most CPU time
Which cache lines miss most often in loops
Lock wait time per thread in the process

takeaway: Profile heap usage first and fix allocation hotspots with measured changes.
trap: Hand-pooling objects before profiling adds complexity without proven gains.
